newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian foreign debt under control-finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Indian foreign debt under control-finance minister.

text.p: India has cut its foreign debt to the lowest level in three years, shaving more than $6 billion from external obligations in the past year and bringing them under control, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said on Friday.
The minister told a parliamentary committee that outstanding external debt fell to $92.6 billion in March, $6.4 billion below the peak of $99 billion in March 1995 and the lowest since 1993.
The country's debt servicing ratio -- debt service payments as a percentage of exports of goods and services -- also fell, according to a government summary of Chidambaram's remarks.
In a recent report, the World Bank classified India as "moderately indebted," and said its external debt was more than twice the value of the country's exports.

In an annual report on the economy released in March, the government of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao said that "the high level of external debt is a matter of continuous concern for the government."

At that time, the government said debt service payments as a percentage of exports had risen to 26.7 percent from 25.1 percent in March 1995, higher than the ratio for most other developing countries.
But Chidambaram, who was named finance minister after Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda took office in June, said that "...the government was in control of the situation," the statement said.

Earlier this week, Chidambaram said India's debt service ratio, reflecting the nation's ability to repay its debts, had declined to 26 percent. But he said it needed eventually to be trimmed to 20 percent.
Addressing concerns that industrial growth was being strangled by the relatively high cost of money, Chidambaram told the lawmakers that "the government would endeavour to bring down interest rates."
He said the "liquidity crunch had eased considerably and there were adequate reserves of foreign exchange for imports."
Domestic industry has complained that tight liquidity along with high interest rates has hampered economic growth.

But Chidambaram said the government expected India's gross domestic product to grow by about seven percent in the 1996/97 financial year that began on April 1, the same rate of expansion as in 1995/96.
He said industrial production grew 11.5 percent in May compared to the same month in 1995, and sluggish growth was concentrated in industries regulated by the government.
"Perhaps there was need to remove those regulations which hindered growth," the statement quoted Chidambaram as saying.
